qs.prompt: La girafe est ___ grande ___ le chien.
qs.en: The giraffe is taller than the dog.

qs.prompt: Ce livre est ___ intéressant ___ le film.
qs.en: The book is as interesting as the film.

qs.prompt: Ma voiture est ___ rapide ___ le train.
qs.en: My car is less fast than the train.

qs.prompt: Batman mange ___ chips que Superman.
qs.en: Batman eats more chips than Superman.
qs.note: With a NOUN, use plus DE / moins DE / autant DE + noun + que.

qs.prompt: Je dors ___ mon frère.
qs.en: I sleep more than my brother.
qs.note: With a VERB, use verb + plus/moins/autant + que — no 'de'.

qs.prompt: Le thé est ___ ___ le café. (bon)
qs.en: The tea is better than the coffee.
qs.note: EXCEPTION: plus bon(ne) → meilleur(e). Never say 'plus bon'.

qs.prompt: Ce restaurant est ___ ___ l'autre. (mauvais)
qs.en: This restaurant is worse than the other.
opts: pire que ou plus mauvais que (les deux)
qs.note: plus mauvais → pire. BOTH are correct.

qs.prompt: Pierre est plus grand ___ sa sœur.
qs.en: Pierre is taller than his sister.
qs.note: The second part is always 'que', not 'de'.

qs.prompt: Marie est aussi rapide ___ Léo.
qs.en: Marie is as fast as Léo.
qs.note: aussi ... QUE — never 'comme' for comparisons of equality.

qs.prompt: Il y a ___ neige à Morzine ___ à Paris.
qs.en: There is more snow in Morzine than in Paris.
qs.note: plus DE neige que — remember 'de' before the noun.

qs.prompt: Je ___ apprendre à skier hors-piste.
qs.en: I want to learn to ski off-piste.
qs.note: vouloir = desire. Je veux = I want.

qs.prompt: Vous ___ montrer votre forfait à l'entrée.
qs.en: You must show your ski pass at the entrance.
qs.note: devoir = obligation. Vous devez = you must.

qs.prompt: Nous ___ réserver une table ?
qs.en: Must we book a table?

qs.prompt: On ne ___ pas skier aujourd'hui — les pistes sont fermées.
qs.en: We can't ski today — the pistes are closed.
qs.note: pouvoir = possibility/permission. On peut = we can.

qs.prompt: Tu ___ m'appeler si tu te perds ?
qs.en: Can you call me if you get lost?
qs.note: pouvoir = ability. Tu peux = you can.

qs.prompt: Elle ___ absolument essayer le snowboard !
qs.en: She absolutely wants to try snowboarding!

qs.prompt: Ils ___ louer un appartement pour la saison.
qs.en: They want to rent an apartment for the season.

qs.prompt: Il ___ aller au spa — il a mal aux jambes.
qs.en: He wants to go to the spa — his legs hurt.
qs.note: The reason (sore legs) signals wanting, though 'doit' is also plausible. The lesson answer is 'veut'.

qs.prompt: Je ___ parler français.
qs.en: I can speak French.
qs.note: For ability 'I can', 'je peux' is used. (Some contexts prefer 'je sais parler' for skills, but pouvoir is the lesson answer.)

qs.prompt: On ___ porter un casque sur les pistes.
qs.en: We must wear a helmet on the pistes.

qs.prompt: Les lunettes, elles sont à toi ? — Oui, ce sont ___ lunettes.
qs.en: The glasses, are they yours? — Yes, they are my glasses.

qs.prompt: Le panda, il est à lui ? — Oui, c'est ___ panda.
qs.en: The panda, is it his? — Yes, it's his panda.

qs.prompt: Vos enfants torturent mon chien ? — Oui, ce sont ___ enfants.
qs.en: Your children are torturing my dog? — Yes, they are our children.

qs.prompt: C'est la voiture de Jean et Brigitte ? — Oui, c'est ___ voiture.
qs.en: Is it Jean and Brigitte's car? — Yes, it's their car.
qs.note: TWO owners → leur. 'voiture' is singular, so leur (not leurs).

qs.prompt: J'ai oublié ___ chaussettes.
qs.en: I forgot my socks.

qs.prompt: Est-ce que je peux inviter ___ voisins à notre mariage ?
qs.en: Can I invite my neighbours to our wedding?

qs.prompt: J'ai adopté un tigre ! Je vais te montrer ___ photo.
qs.en: I adopted a tiger! I'll show you its photo.
qs.note: photo = feminine singular → sa (the tiger's photo).

qs.prompt: Bonjour Monsieur, montrez-moi ___ documents.
qs.en: Hello sir, show me your documents.

qs.prompt: C'est l'amie de Jean qui boit trop de bière ? — Oui, c'est ___ amie.
qs.en: Is that Jean's friend who drinks too much beer? — Yes, it's his friend.
qs.note: Tricky: 'amie' is feminine BUT begins with a vowel → son (not sa) to avoid the vowel clash. Same as 'mon école'.

qs.prompt: Pourquoi ils sont heureux ? Parce qu'ils ont réussi ___ examen.
qs.en: Why are they happy? Because they passed their exam.

qs.prompt: ___ regardes-tu ce film ? — Parce que j'aime les super-héros.
qs.en: Why are you watching this film?

qs.prompt: Cette Porsche coûte ___ ? — Seulement 67 000 €.
qs.en: How much does this Porsche cost?

qs.prompt: Avec ___ est-ce que tu habites ? — Avec mon ami.
qs.en: Who do you live with?

qs.prompt: ___ de chiens as-tu ? — Deux.
qs.en: How many dogs do you have?

qs.prompt: Ton avion part ___ ? — Il part demain matin.
qs.en: When does your plane leave?

qs.prompt: ___ est-ce que tu apprends ? — Pour faire plaisir à mes parents.
qs.en: Why are you learning?

qs.prompt: ___ est ton loisir préféré ? — Le sport.
qs.en: What is your favourite hobby?
qs.note: 'quel' + noun (loisir). Asking to choose among options = quel.

qs.prompt: ___ voyagez-vous ? — En avion.
qs.en: How do you travel?

qs.prompt: Tu fais ___ ? — Je surfe sur Internet.
qs.en: What are you doing?
qs.note: 'Tu fais quoi' = informal. 'Qu'est-ce que tu fais' uses que/qu'.

qs.prompt: Quand tu as très faim, tu manges ___ ? — Des croissants.
qs.en: What do you eat when very hungry?
qs.note: Thing → quoi. At end of question = quoi (not que).

qs.prompt: Je vais ___ au collège à pied.
qs.en: I often go to school on foot.

qs.prompt: Il ne pleut ___ en été dans cette région.
qs.en: It never rains in summer here.

qs.prompt: ___ nous allons faire les devoirs, ___ nous pourrons jouer.
qs.en: Now we'll do homework, then we can play.

qs.prompt: Je vais ___ terminer cet exercice !
qs.en: I'm finally going to finish this exercise!

qs.prompt: ___, il faut lire la consigne.
qs.en: First, you must read the instructions.

qs.prompt: Ce matin, je me réveille ___ très tôt.
qs.en: This morning, I wake up first thing very early.

qs.prompt: ___, je prends mon petit-déjeuner.
qs.en: Next, I have breakfast.

qs.prompt: Mon frère est ___ en retard !
qs.en: My brother is always late!

qs.prompt: Moi, je suis ___ ponctuel.
qs.en: Me, I'm often punctual.

qs.prompt: ___, nous partons ensemble.
qs.en: Finally, we leave together.

roleplays.title: À la boulangerie
roleplays.ctx: You walk into the bakery in Morzine for your morning bread.

lines.fr: Bonjour monsieur, qu'est-ce que je vous sers ?
lines.en: Hello sir, what can I get you?

lines.fr: Bonjour ! Je voudrais une baguette, s'il vous plaît.
lines.en: Hello! I'd like a baguette, please.

lines.fr: Tradition ou classique ?
lines.en: Tradition or classic?

lines.fr: Une tradition, merci. Et deux croissants aussi.
lines.en: A tradition, thanks. And two croissants as well.

lines.fr: Très bien. Ce sera tout ?
lines.en: Very good. Will that be all?

lines.fr: Oui, c'est tout. Ça fait combien ?
lines.en: Yes, that's all. How much is it?

lines.fr: Cinq euros quarante, s'il vous plaît.
lines.en: Five euros forty, please.

lines.fr: Voilà. Bonne journée !
lines.en: Here you go. Have a good day!

roleplays.notes: Je voudrais is the polite form of je veux — always use it in shops and restaurants. The reply to 'ça fait combien?' is pure listening practice — numbers are the hardest part of French retail.

roleplays.title: Au magasin de location de ski
roleplays.ctx: You're renting skis for the week.

lines.fr: Bonjour ! Je peux vous aider ?
lines.en: Hello! Can I help you?

lines.fr: Oui, je voudrais louer des skis pour la semaine.
lines.en: Yes, I'd like to rent skis for the week.

lines.fr: Quel est votre niveau ?
lines.en: What's your level?

lines.fr: Intermédiaire. Je veux skier sur les pistes rouges.
lines.en: Intermediate. I want to ski on red pistes.

lines.fr: Très bien. Vous faites quelle taille ?
lines.en: Very good. What's your size?

lines.fr: Un mètre quatre-vingts. Et je dois aussi louer un casque.
lines.en: 1m80. And I also need to rent a helmet.

lines.fr: Pas de problème. Vous devez signer ici.
lines.en: No problem. You must sign here.

lines.fr: D'accord. Je peux payer par carte ?
lines.en: OK. Can I pay by card?

roleplays.notes: Great use of all three modals: je voudrais (polite want), je dois (obligation), je peux (asking permission). Quel est votre niveau ? — memorise this full phrase.

roleplays.title: Au restaurant de montagne
roleplays.ctx: Lunch at a mountain restaurant like Le Pleney after a morning's skiing.

lines.fr: Bonjour, vous avez réservé ?
lines.en: Hello, do you have a reservation?

lines.fr: Non, nous sommes deux. On peut manger en terrasse ?
lines.en: No, we're two people. Can we eat on the terrace?

lines.fr: Oui, suivez-moi. Voici la carte.
lines.en: Yes, follow me. Here's the menu.

lines.fr: Merci. Qu'est-ce que vous recommandez ?
lines.en: Thanks. What do you recommend?

lines.fr: La tartiflette est excellente aujourd'hui.
lines.en: The tartiflette is excellent today.

lines.fr: Parfait. Deux tartiflettes et deux bières, s'il vous plaît.
lines.en: Perfect. Two tartiflettes and two beers, please.

lines.fr: Très bien. Ce sera tout ?
lines.en: Very good. Will that be all?

lines.fr: Oui, pour l'instant. Merci !
lines.en: Yes, for now. Thanks!

roleplays.notes: Note on peut — in spoken French, 'on' replaces 'nous' in almost all situations. Suivez-moi is the imperative vous-form of suivre (to follow). Ce sera tout ? is stock restaurant phrasing — you'll hear it constantly.

roleplays.title: Au bar, après le ski
roleplays.ctx: Meeting someone at a bar in town for an après-ski drink.

lines.fr: Salut ! Qu'est-ce que tu as fait aujourd'hui ?
lines.en: Hi! What did you do today?

lines.fr: Salut ! J'ai skié toute la journée. Et toi ?
lines.en: Hi! I skied all day. And you?

lines.fr: Moi aussi ! Les pistes étaient super.
lines.en: Me too! The pistes were great.

lines.fr: Oui, mais il y a plus de monde que la semaine dernière.
lines.en: Yes, but there are more people than last week.

lines.fr: C'est vrai. Tu veux boire quelque chose ?
lines.en: That's true. Do you want something to drink?

lines.fr: Oui, je voudrais une bière, s'il te plaît. Et toi ?
lines.en: Yes, I'd like a beer please. And you?

lines.fr: Un vin chaud pour moi. On commande ?
lines.en: A mulled wine for me. Shall we order?

roleplays.notes: Il y a plus de monde que... uses the comparison rule for nouns: plus DE + noun + que. Note s'il te plaît (tu) vs s'il vous plaît (vous) — you'll use 'te' with someone you know well.

roleplays.title: Chez le voisin
roleplays.ctx: A neighbour knocks at your chalet door.

lines.fr: Bonjour ! Excusez-moi de vous déranger.
lines.en: Hello! Sorry to bother you.

lines.fr: Pas de problème. Qu'est-ce qui se passe ?
lines.en: No problem. What's going on?

lines.fr: C'est votre voiture, la rouge ? Elle bloque la sortie.
lines.en: Is that your car, the red one? It's blocking the exit.

lines.fr: Oui, c'est ma voiture. Désolé, je la déplace tout de suite.
lines.en: Yes, that's my car. Sorry, I'll move it right away.

lines.fr: Merci beaucoup !
lines.en: Thank you very much!

lines.fr: Au fait, comment vous vous appelez ? Je m'appelle Martyn.
lines.en: By the way, what's your name? I'm Martyn.

lines.fr: Moi, c'est Pierre. Enchanté !
lines.en: I'm Pierre. Nice to meet you!

roleplays.notes: Qu'est-ce qui se passe ? = 'what's happening' — very useful phrase. Je la déplace tout de suite uses the object pronoun 'la' (meaning 'it' referring to the car). Au fait = by the way.

roleplays.title: À l'office de tourisme
roleplays.ctx: You've just arrived in Morzine and need information.

lines.fr: Bonjour ! On peut faire du ski aujourd'hui ?
lines.en: Hello! Can one go skiing today?

lines.fr: Oui, vous pouvez skier sur 15 pistes !
lines.en: Yes, you can ski on 15 pistes!

lines.fr: Est-ce qu'on doit réserver à l'avance ?
lines.en: Do we need to book in advance?

lines.fr: Vous devez acheter un forfait, mais vous pouvez le faire en ligne.
lines.en: You must buy a pass, but you can do it online.

lines.fr: On peut louer des skis ici ?
lines.en: Can we rent skis here?

lines.fr: Vous pouvez louer au magasin Morzine Sports, à deux minutes à pied.
lines.en: You can rent at Morzine Sports, two minutes on foot.

lines.fr: Parfait, merci beaucoup !
lines.en: Perfect, thank you very much!

roleplays.notes: Straight from your lesson sheet. Classic back-and-forth of on peut / vous pouvez (possibility) and on doit / vous devez (obligation). Notice the polite 'vous' from the tourism office.

roleplays.title: Comparer la vie ici
roleplays.ctx: Chatting with a French friend about how Morzine compares to your old life.

lines.fr: Tu préfères vivre ici ou en Angleterre ?
lines.en: Do you prefer living here or in England?

lines.fr: J'aime beaucoup Morzine. C'est plus calme qu'en Angleterre.
lines.en: I love Morzine. It's calmer than in England.

lines.fr: Et la nourriture ?
lines.en: And the food?

lines.fr: La nourriture française est meilleure ! Mais le thé est moins bon.
lines.en: French food is better! But the tea is less good.

lines.fr: Haha ! Et le travail ?
lines.en: Haha! And work?

lines.fr: Je travaille autant qu'avant, mais je suis plus heureux.
lines.en: I work as much as before, but I'm happier.

lines.fr: C'est l'essentiel !
lines.en: That's what matters!

roleplays.notes: This one is a workout for comparisons: plus calme que (adjective), meilleure (exception for 'plus bonne'), moins bon (correct — 'pire' is only for 'plus mauvais'), autant que (verb comparison = as much as). Use 'plus heureux' because 'bon' ≠ happy.

grammar.title: The comparison — plus / moins / aussi
grammar.body:
The formula depends on what type of word follows:

With an adjective or adverbplus / moins / aussi + adjective + que
Il est plus grand que son frère.
With a verbverb + plus / moins / autant + que (no 'de')
Je dors plus que toi.
With a nounplus de / moins de / autant de + noun + que
J'ai plus de neige que toi.

Exceptions: never say 'plus bon' — use meilleur(e). And 'plus mauvais' can become pire.

grammar.title: Modal verbs — pouvoir, devoir, vouloir
grammar.body:
These three do almost all the heavy lifting in everyday conversation. Each is followed by an infinitive.

pouvoirdevoirvouloir
jepeuxdoisveux
tupeuxdoisveux
il/ellepeutdoitveut
nouspouvonsdevonsvoulons
vouspouvezdevezvoulez
ils/ellespeuventdoiventveulent

pouvoir = can / be able to / permission · devoir = must / have to · vouloir = want

Tip: je voudrais (conditional of vouloir) = 'I would like'. Use it in shops, restaurants, anywhere polite. You never ask for things with 'je veux' — it sounds rude.

grammar.title: Possessive adjectives — mon, ton, son...
grammar.body:
They agree with the thing owned, not the owner.

masc. sing.fem. sing.plural
mymonmames
your (tu)tontates
his/hersonsases
ournotrenos
your (vous)votrevos
theirleurleurs

Critical rule: before a feminine word starting with a vowel (or silent h), use the masculine form for sound. So it's mon école, son amie, ton histoire — not ma/sa/ta.

son vs leur: son/sa/ses = one owner; leur/leurs = multiple owners. 'La voiture de Jean et Brigitte' → c'est leur voiture (two owners, one car).

grammar.title: Question words
grammar.body:
Three ways to ask a question: rising intonation ('Tu viens ?'), est-ce que, or inversion ('Viens-tu ?').

WordMeaningExample
quiwhoQui parle ?
quoi / quewhatTu fais quoi ?
oùwhereOù vas-tu ?
quandwhenQuand pars-tu ?
pourquoiwhyPourquoi ?
commenthowComment ça va ?
combien (de)how much/manyCombien ça coûte ?
quel(le/s)which/whatQuel âge as-tu ?

Quel agrees with its noun: quel (m), quelle (f), quels/quelles (pl).

grammar.title: Adverbs of time & sequence
grammar.body:
These are your discourse glue — they connect sentences into real narrative.

Sequence d'abord (first) → ensuite (next) / puis (then) → enfin (finally)
Frequency toujours (always) · souvent (often) · parfois (sometimes) · jamais (never)
Time & consequence maintenant (now) · alors (so/then)

Jamais usually pairs with ne: Je ne mange jamais de viande.

grammar.title: Pronunciation cheats
grammar.body:
The things that trip up English speakers most in Morzine conversations:

Silent endings: final consonants are usually silent. Parlent sounds like 'parl'. Veulent sounds like 'veul'. Ils peuvent sounds like 'il peuv'.

Liaisons: a silent final consonant activates when the next word starts with a vowel. Vous avez → 'vooz-avay'. Les amis → 'layz-amee'.

The -ent ending on verbs is silent. Ils mangent = 'eel monzh'. Elles dansent = 'ell donss'.

R is pronounced at the back of the throat, not rolled. Think of clearing your throat softly.

U vs OU: 'tu' and 'tout' are different sounds. U = round your lips and say 'ee'. OU = English 'oo'.

grammar.title: Mistakes to watch for
grammar.body:
Based on your own lesson sheets — these are your patterns:

Word order with 'plus de + noun': it's Jules fait moins DE sport QUE Annabelle — not 'Jules fait sport moins que'. The 'de' comes before the noun.

Plus bon → meilleur: never say 'plus bon'. It's always meilleur(e).

Son amie, not sa amie: feminine word starting with a vowel → use the masculine form. son amie, mon école, ton histoire.

Leur vs son: when two people own one thing, it's leur, not son/sa. La voiture de Jean et Brigitte → leur voiture.

Conjugate after vouloir/pouvoir/devoir: the second verb stays as infinitive. Je veux aller — not 'je veux va'. Elle veut aller au ski, not 'elle veut au ski'.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I want a coffee, please.
dailyDrills.fr: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
dailyDrills.note: Je voudrais is the polite form of je veux.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Can you help me?
dailyDrills.note: 'vous pouvez' — polite, stock phrase.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I have to go to the supermarket.
dailyDrills.note: devoir + infinitive.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I ski more than my brother.
dailyDrills.fr: Je skie plus que mon frère.
dailyDrills.note: verb + plus + que (no 'de' with a verb).

dailyDrills.en: Say: There are more people here than yesterday.
dailyDrills.fr: Il y a plus de monde ici qu'hier.
dailyDrills.note: plus DE + noun + que.

dailyDrills.en: Say: This restaurant is better than the other.
dailyDrills.fr: Ce restaurant est meilleur que l'autre.
dailyDrills.note: meilleur, not 'plus bon'.

dailyDrills.en: Say: My neighbours are really nice.
dailyDrills.note: plural noun → mes + plural adjective (sympas).

dailyDrills.en: Say: I never work on Sundays.
dailyDrills.fr: Je ne travaille jamais le dimanche.
dailyDrills.note: ne + verb + jamais sandwich.

dailyDrills.en: Say: First I eat breakfast, then I go to work.
dailyDrills.fr: D'abord je prends mon petit-déjeuner, puis je vais au travail.
dailyDrills.note: d'abord ... puis — connects steps.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I would like to try the raclette.
dailyDrills.note: Polite want + infinitive.

dailyDrills.en: Say: Sorry, I don't understand.
dailyDrills.note: Use this constantly. No shame.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I'm learning French because I live in Morzine.
dailyDrills.fr: J'apprends le français parce que j'habite à Morzine.
dailyDrills.note: parce que = because.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I have been here for two years.
dailyDrills.fr: Je suis ici depuis deux ans.
dailyDrills.note: depuis = 'for' (ongoing time).

dailyDrills.en: Say: It's too expensive for me.
dailyDrills.note: trop = too (much).

dailyDrills.en: Ask: What time does it open?
dailyDrills.note: à quelle heure — one chunk.

dailyDrills.en: Say: The pistes are closed today.
dailyDrills.note: fermées agrees with 'les pistes' (fem. pl.).

dailyDrills.en: Say: Hello, nice to meet you.
dailyDrills.note: Women say 'enchantée'. Shake hands; use 'bise' (cheek kisses) with friends.

dailyDrills.en: Say: My name is Martyn.
dailyDrills.note: Literally 'I call myself' — reflexive verb.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: What's your name?
dailyDrills.note: Informal version: Comment tu t'appelles ?

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Where do you come from?
dailyDrills.note: Or more formal: D'où venez-vous ?

dailyDrills.en: Say: I'm English but I live here.
dailyDrills.fr: Je suis anglais mais j'habite ici.
dailyDrills.note: Women say 'anglaise'. No 'un/une' before nationality.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I live in Morzine for two years.
dailyDrills.fr: J'habite à Morzine depuis deux ans.
dailyDrills.note: depuis + present tense = ongoing 'for'.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: What do you do (for work)?
dailyDrills.fr: Qu'est-ce que vous faites dans la vie ?
dailyDrills.note: Literally 'what do you do in life'. Very natural phrasing.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I run a business, I'm a director.
dailyDrills.fr: Je dirige une entreprise, je suis directeur.
dailyDrills.note: No 'un' before profession. 'Directrice' if female.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: How long have you lived here?
dailyDrills.fr: Depuis combien de temps vous habitez ici ?
dailyDrills.note: Literally 'since how much time' — the French way.

dailyDrills.en: Say: It's a pleasure to meet you.
dailyDrills.note: 'Ravi' = delighted. Women: 'ravie'.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Do you have children?
dailyDrills.note: 'des' = some (the plural indefinite).

dailyDrills.en: Say: We can switch to 'tu' if you like.
dailyDrills.fr: On peut se tutoyer, si tu veux.
dailyDrills.note: 'se tutoyer' = to address each other informally. Big social moment in France.

dailyDrills.en: Say: Excuse me for my bad French!
dailyDrills.note: Disarming and polite. Always gets a smile.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Can you speak more slowly please?
dailyDrills.fr: Vous pouvez parler plus lentement, s'il vous plaît ?
dailyDrills.note: plus lentement = more slowly. Essential.

dailyDrills.en: Say: See you soon!
dailyDrills.note: Or: à plus tard (later), à demain (tomorrow).

dailyDrills.en: Say: Hello, I'm just looking.
dailyDrills.note: Polite brush-off when you don't want help immediately.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Do you have this in another size?
dailyDrills.fr: Vous avez ça dans une autre taille ?
dailyDrills.note: taille = size (clothes). For shoes say 'pointure'.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Can I try it on?
dailyDrills.note: 'l'' = it (replaces the object). 'essayer' = to try.

dailyDrills.en: Say: It's too small.
dailyDrills.note: trop = too. For 'too big' → trop grand.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: How much does it cost?
dailyDrills.note: Or: combien ça coûte / c'est combien.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I'll think about it, thanks.
dailyDrills.note: Graceful exit. 'réfléchir' = to think about.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I'll take it.
dailyDrills.note: Use 'la prends' for feminine items. 'le' / 'la' = it.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Can I pay by card?
dailyDrills.note: pouvoir = permission. Usually yes in France now.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Do you have a bag?
dailyDrills.note: Most shops charge a few cents. Often they ask first.

dailyDrills.en: Say: No bag, thanks, I have one.
dailyDrills.note: 'en' = 'of them / one of those'. Tricky but useful.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Do you have a loyalty card?
dailyDrills.fr: Vous avez une carte de fidélité ?
dailyDrills.note: They'll ask YOU this all the time. Answer: non merci.

dailyDrills.en: Say: Can you gift-wrap it?
dailyDrills.fr: Vous pouvez me faire un paquet cadeau ?
dailyDrills.note: Free in most French shops, very common.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Is there a discount?
dailyDrills.note: réduction = discount. Or 'solde' during sale periods.

dailyDrills.en: Say: That's all, thanks.
dailyDrills.note: Stock phrase at the till. 'Sera' is future of être.

dailyDrills.en: Say: Here you go (handing over money).
dailyDrills.note: Magic word. Works for 'here you are', 'there you go', 'done'.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Where is the bread?
dailyDrills.note: Or: 'Où se trouve le pain ?' (literally 'where finds itself').

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Where is the dairy section?
dailyDrills.note: 'rayon' = aisle / section. Rayon boucherie, rayon fromage, etc.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I'm looking for baking powder.
dailyDrills.fr: Je cherche de la levure chimique.
dailyDrills.note: chercher = to look for (don't translate 'for'). Useful: 'je cherche...'.

dailyDrills.en: Say: Do you have any fresh milk?
dailyDrills.note: French default is UHT; 'frais' = fresh. In the cold section.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: How much is the reblochon?
dailyDrills.note: You can also just hand it to them and they'll tell you.

dailyDrills.en: Say: Two hundred grams, please.
dailyDrills.fr: Deux cents grammes, s'il vous plaît.
dailyDrills.note: At the cheese or deli counter. 200g = classic portion.

dailyDrills.en: Say: A slice of ham, thin please.
dailyDrills.fr: Une tranche de jambon, fine s'il vous plaît.
dailyDrills.note: tranche = slice. 'fine' = thin (feminine agrees with tranche).

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Is it a ripe (ready-to-eat) one?
dailyDrills.note: For fruit/cheese. 'mûr' = ripe. Essential for French cheese shopping.

dailyDrills.en: Say: Can I have a bag for my vegetables?
dailyDrills.fr: Je peux avoir un sac pour mes légumes ?
dailyDrills.note: Many supermarkets have paper bags at the scales.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I don't have change.
dailyDrills.note: 'monnaie' = coins/change, NOT 'argent' (money in general).

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Do you accept contactless?
dailyDrills.note: 'sans contact' = contactless. Nearly everywhere does.

dailyDrills.en: Say: The receipt, please.
dailyDrills.note: 'ticket' (not 'reçu') for supermarket receipts.

dailyDrills.en: Say: Is this self-service?
dailyDrills.note: libre-service = self-service. At cheese / charcuterie sometimes.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I'll put my basket back.
dailyDrills.note: panier = basket, chariot = trolley. 'remettre' = to put back.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: What's this? (pointing)
dailyDrills.note: Very informal but totally fine. Point, they'll explain.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Do you have a table for two?
dailyDrills.fr: Vous avez une table pour deux ?
dailyDrills.note: Add 'en terrasse' if you want outside.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I'll have a beer please.
dailyDrills.fr: Je vais prendre une bière, s'il vous plaît.
dailyDrills.note: 'Je vais prendre' = 'I'll have'. More natural than 'je veux'.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: What do you have on draft?
dailyDrills.fr: Qu'est-ce que vous avez à la pression ?
dailyDrills.note: 'à la pression' = on draft/tap.

dailyDrills.en: Say: A small / large beer please.
dailyDrills.fr: Un demi / une pinte, s'il vous plaît.
dailyDrills.note: 'un demi' = 25cl (standard French size). 'une pinte' = 50cl.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: What do you recommend?
dailyDrills.note: Always get a good answer. 'me' = to me.

dailyDrills.en: Say: The same for me.
dailyDrills.note: Or: 'Moi aussi' / 'pareil'. Handy in groups.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Is it spicy?
dailyDrills.note: French food is rarely very spicy, but good to check.

dailyDrills.en: Say: I'm allergic to nuts.
dailyDrills.fr: Je suis allergique aux fruits à coque.
dailyDrills.note: 'fruits à coque' = tree nuts. 'aux arachides' = peanuts.

dailyDrills.en: Say: Rare / medium / well done.
dailyDrills.note: For steak. 'Saignant' literally = bleeding. French 'well done' is still pinker than UK.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Can we have the menu?
dailyDrills.note: 'la carte' = menu. 'Le menu' = fixed-price set menu.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Can we have some water please?
dailyDrills.fr: Une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît ?
dailyDrills.note: 'carafe' = free tap water. 'Eau plate/gazeuse' = still/sparkling (paid).

dailyDrills.en: Say: That was delicious.
dailyDrills.note: 'était' = past tense of être. Staff love hearing this.

dailyDrills.en: Ask: Can we have the bill?
dailyDrills.note: 'addition' = bill. Never ask for 'la facture' in a restaurant — that's a commercial invoice.

dailyDrills.en: Say: Keep the change.
dailyDrills.note: French tipping is small and optional. 1-2€ on drinks is generous.

dailyDrills.en: Say: Cheers!
dailyDrills.note: Look everyone in the eye when you clink — it's a real thing in France.

stories.title: Une matinée à Morzine
stories.blurb: A simple morning routine — sequence words, daily verbs
focus: D'abord, ensuite, puis, enfin — the sequence glue
Present tense of être, avoir, faire, aller, prendre
stories.body:
[[Tous les matins|Every morning|the 's' on 'matin' makes it plural]], je me [[réveille|wake up|reflexive verb]] à sept heures. [[D'abord|First]], je [[prends|take / have|'prendre' = to take]] une douche [[chaude|hot|adjective agrees with 'douche' (fem.)]], [[puis|then]] je [[descends|go down]] dans la cuisine.

[[Ensuite|Next]], je [[prépare|prepare]] mon petit-déjeuner. [[Aujourd'hui|Today]], je [[mange|eat]] du [[pain|bread]] avec du [[beurre|butter]] et de la [[confiture|jam]]. Je [[bois|drink|'boire' = to drink]] aussi un café. Il est très [[fort|strong]] !

[[Après|After]], je [[regarde|look at / watch]] par la [[fenêtre|window]]. Les [[montagnes|mountains]] sont [[magnifiques|magnificent]] [[quand|when]] il y a de la [[neige|snow]]. [[Parfois|Sometimes]], je [[vois|see|'voir' = to see]] des [[skieurs|skiers]] sur les pistes.

[[Enfin|Finally]], je [[mets|put on|'mettre' = to put]] mes [[bottes|boots]] et ma [[veste|jacket]], et je [[sors|go out|'sortir' = to leave/go out]]. Il fait [[froid|cold]], mais je suis [[content|happy]]. La [[journée|day]] [[commence bien|starts well]] !
stories.translation:
Every morning, I wake up at seven. First, I take a hot shower, then I go down to the kitchen.

Next, I prepare my breakfast. Today, I'm eating bread with butter and jam. I also drink a coffee. It's very strong!

After, I look out of the window. The mountains are magnificent when there is snow. Sometimes, I see skiers on the slopes.

Finally, I put on my boots and my jacket, and I go out. It's cold, but I'm happy. The day starts well!

stories.title: Au marché du mercredi
focus: Comparisons with adjectives: plus … que, moins … que, aussi … que
stories.body:
[[Le mercredi matin|Wednesday morning]], je [[vais|go]] au marché à Morzine. Il y a [[beaucoup de|lots of]] [[monde|people]] et [[beaucoup de choses|lots of things]] à [[acheter|buy]].

[[D'abord|First]], je [[choisis|choose|'choisir' = to choose]] des [[fruits|fruits]]. Les [[pommes|apples]] sont [[plus chères que|more expensive than]] la [[semaine dernière|last week]], mais elles sont [[meilleures|better|exception: NEVER 'plus bonnes']] ! Le [[vendeur|seller / vendor]] est très [[sympa|nice]].

[[Ensuite|Next]], je [[regarde|look at]] les [[fromages|cheeses]]. Il y a [[plus de choix|more choice|'plus DE' + noun]] ici [[qu'au|than at the|qu' = que + vowel]] [[supermarché|supermarket]]. Le [[reblochon|reblochon (Alpine cheese)]] est [[délicieux|delicious]] et [[moins cher qu'à Paris|cheaper than in Paris]].

[[Après|After]], je [[prends|buy / take]] du [[pain|bread]] à la [[boulangerie|bakery]]. La [[baguette tradition|traditional baguette]] est [[aussi bonne que|as good as]] celle de ma [[boulangerie préférée|favourite bakery]].

[[À la fin|At the end]], [[mon sac est plus lourd que|my bag is heavier than]] [[d'habitude|usual]] ! [[Mais ça va|But it's fine]] — [[je mange mieux|I eat better]] [[quand|when]] je [[cuisine|cook]] [[moi-même|myself]]. [[La prochaine fois|Next time]], je [[veux|want]] [[essayer|to try]] le [[saucisson|dry sausage]].
stories.translation:
Wednesday morning, I go to the market in Morzine. There are lots of people and lots of things to buy.

First, I choose some fruits. The apples are more expensive than last week, but they are better! The vendor is very nice.

Next, I look at the cheeses. There's more choice here than at the supermarket. The reblochon is delicious and cheaper than in Paris.

After, I get some bread at the bakery. The traditional baguette is as good as the one from my favourite bakery.

At the end, my bag is heavier than usual! But it's fine — I eat better when I cook myself. Next time, I want to try the dry sausage.

stories.title: La première leçon de ski
stories.blurb: Pierre's first ski lesson — modal verbs in action
stories.body:
Pierre [[est arrivé|arrived|passé composé with être]] à Morzine [[hier soir|last night]]. C'est la [[première fois|first time]] qu'il [[essaie|tries]] le ski. [[Ce matin|This morning]], il [[doit|must]] [[aller|go]] au magasin [[pour|to / in order to]] [[louer|rent]] [[son équipement|his equipment]].

— [[Bonjour|Hello]] ! [[Je voudrais|I would like|polite form of 'je veux']] [[louer|to rent]] des skis, [[dit-il|he says]] [[au vendeur|to the seller]].

— [[Bien sûr|Of course]]. [[Quel est votre niveau|What's your level]] ?

— [[Je suis débutant|I'm a beginner]]. [[Je ne peux pas|I can't|pouvoir + infinitive]] [[encore|yet]] [[skier|ski]] sur les pistes [[difficiles|difficult]].

— [[Pas de problème|No problem]]. Vous [[devez|must]] [[prendre|take]] des skis [[courts|short]]. Et vous [[devez absolument|must absolutely]] [[porter|wear]] un [[casque|helmet]] !

Pierre [[veut aussi|also wants]] [[acheter|to buy]] un [[forfait|ski pass]]. Il [[peut|can]] [[skier|ski]] sur [[quinze pistes|fifteen pistes]] [[pendant|during]] [[trois jours|three days]]. [[C'est parfait|It's perfect]] !

[[Plus tard|Later]], à [[l'école de ski|the ski school]], son [[moniteur|instructor]] [[lui dit|says to him]] :

— [[Tu peux|You can]] [[essayer|try]] [[doucement|gently]]. [[Si tu tombes|If you fall]], [[tu dois|you must]] [[te relever|get yourself up]] [[sans paniquer|without panicking]]. [[Et si|And if]] [[tu as peur|you're afraid]], [[tu peux|you can]] [[m'appeler|call me]].

[[À la fin de la journée|At the end of the day]], Pierre est [[fatigué|tired]] mais [[heureux|happy]]. Il [[veut|wants]] [[revenir|to come back]] [[demain|tomorrow]] !
stories.translation:
Pierre arrived in Morzine last night. It's the first time he's trying skiing. This morning, he must go to the shop to rent his equipment.

— "Hello! I would like to rent some skis," he says to the seller.

— "Of course. What's your level?"

— "I'm a beginner. I can't yet ski on the difficult pistes."

— "No problem. You must take short skis. And you must absolutely wear a helmet!"

Pierre also wants to buy a ski pass. He can ski on fifteen pistes during three days. It's perfect!

Later, at the ski school, his instructor says to him:

— "You can try gently. If you fall, you must get up without panicking. And if you're afraid, you can call me."

At the end of the day, Pierre is tired but happy. He wants to come back tomorrow!

stories.title: La famille de Sophie
stories.blurb: Sophie introduces her family — possessive adjectives
focus: All possessives: mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses, notre/nos, votre/vos, leur/leurs
The trick: son amie (not sa) because 'amie' starts with a vowel
stories.body:
[[Je m'appelle|My name is]] Sophie et [[j'habite|I live]] à Morzine [[avec ma famille|with my family]]. [[Nous sommes|We are]] [[quatre|four]] à la [[maison|house]].

[[Mon père|My father]] [[s'appelle|is called]] Thomas. [[Il est médecin|He's a doctor|no 'un' before profession]] à l'[[hôpital|hospital]] de [[Thonon|Thonon (a nearby town)]]. [[Ses patients|His patients]] l'[[aiment bien|like him a lot]] [[parce qu'il|because he]] est [[patient|patient]] et [[sympa|nice]]. [[Il travaille|He works]] [[beaucoup|a lot]], mais [[le week-end|on the weekend]], il [[aime|likes]] [[faire du ski|to go skiing]] [[avec nous|with us]].

[[Ma mère|My mother]] [[s'appelle|is called]] Claire. [[Elle est professeure|She's a teacher]] [[à l'école primaire|at the primary school]]. [[Ses élèves|Her pupils]] sont [[adorables|adorable]] et [[elle adore|she loves]] [[son métier|her job]]. [[Le soir|In the evening]], elle [[lit|reads]] [[ses livres|her books]] devant [[la cheminée|the fireplace]].

[[Mon frère|My brother]] [[s'appelle|is called]] Lucas. [[Il a|He is]] [[quinze ans|fifteen years old|literally "has 15 years"]]. [[Son passe-temps préféré|His favourite hobby]] est [[le snowboard|snowboarding]]. [[Ses amis|His friends]] [[viennent|come]] [[souvent|often]] à la [[maison|house]] pour [[jouer|to play]] aux [[jeux vidéo|video games]].

Et [[moi|me]] ? [[J'ai|I have]] [[une meilleure amie|a best friend (fem.)]] qui [[s'appelle|is called]] Léa. [[C'est ma voisine|She's my neighbour]]. [[Nous aimons|We like]] [[faire nos devoirs|doing our homework]] [[ensemble|together]] et [[partager nos secrets|sharing our secrets]].

[[Mes parents|My parents]] [[ont|have]] aussi [[deux chats|two cats]] : [[leur chat|their cat]] [[s'appelle|is called]] Minou et [[leur chatte|their cat (fem.)]] [[s'appelle|is called]] Poupette. [[Leurs couleurs|Their colours]] [[sont différentes|are different]] mais [[ils dorment|they sleep]] [[toujours ensemble|always together]] !
stories.translation:
My name is Sophie and I live in Morzine with my family. There are four of us at home.

My father is called Thomas. He's a doctor at the hospital in Thonon. His patients like him a lot because he is patient and nice. He works a lot, but on the weekend, he likes to go skiing with us.

My mother is called Claire. She's a teacher at the primary school. Her pupils are adorable and she loves her job. In the evening, she reads her books in front of the fireplace.

My brother is called Lucas. He is fifteen years old. His favourite hobby is snowboarding. His friends often come to the house to play video games.

And me? I have a best friend called Léa. She's my neighbour. We like doing our homework together and sharing our secrets.

My parents also have two cats: their cat is called Minou and their female cat is called Poupette. Their colours are different but they always sleep together!

stories.title: Un dîner entre amis
stories.blurb: A dinner with friends — questions, comparisons, modals
focus: Questions with qui, où, pourquoi, combien, quel, comment
Natural use of modals in conversation
stories.body:
[[Samedi soir|Saturday evening]], [[mes amis et moi|my friends and I]] [[allons dîner|are going to have dinner]] [[au restaurant|at the restaurant]] « Le Clin d'Œil » [[au centre|in the centre]] de Morzine. [[Nous sommes|We are]] [[six|six people]].

[[À l'entrée|At the entrance]], le [[serveur|waiter]] [[nous demande|asks us]] :

— [[Bonsoir|Good evening]] ! [[Vous avez réservé|Have you booked|literally "you have reserved"]] ?

— [[Oui|Yes]], [[au nom de|in the name of]] Martyn, [[pour six personnes|for six people]].

[[Pendant|During]] [[l'apéritif|the aperitif]], [[tout le monde parle|everyone is talking]]. Pierre [[me demande|asks me]] :

— [[Alors|So]], [[pourquoi|why]] [[est-ce que tu as choisi|did you choose]] [[de vivre|to live]] à Morzine ?

— [[Parce que|Because]] [[c'est plus calme|it's calmer]] qu'en [[Angleterre|England]] et les [[montagnes|mountains]] sont [[magnifiques|magnificent]]. [[Et toi|And you]], [[depuis combien de temps|since how long / for how long]] tu [[habites|live]] ici ?

— [[Depuis|For]] [[dix ans|ten years]] ! [[Je ne peux plus|I can no longer|ne … plus = no longer]] [[imaginer|imagine]] [[vivre ailleurs|living elsewhere]].

[[Quand|When]] le [[serveur|waiter]] [[revient|comes back|'revenir' = to come back]], [[il demande|he asks]] :

— [[Qu'est-ce que vous voulez|What do you want / would you like]] [[manger|to eat]] ? [[Je vous recommande|I recommend you]] la [[fondue savoyarde|Savoyard fondue]] — [[c'est notre spécialité|it's our specialty]].

— [[Combien ça coûte|How much does it cost]] ? [[demande|asks]] Julie.

— [[Vingt-cinq euros|Twenty-five euros]] [[par personne|per person]].

— [[C'est un peu cher|It's a bit expensive]], [[mais on doit|but we must]] [[essayer|try]] [[au moins une fois|at least once]] !

Le [[repas|meal]] est [[délicieux|delicious]]. [[Nous mangeons plus|We eat more]] et [[parlons plus fort|talk louder]] [[que d'habitude|than usual]]. [[À la fin|At the end]], Martyn [[dit|says]] :

— [[C'est la meilleure soirée|It's the best evening]] [[de la semaine|of the week]] ! [[Qui veut|Who wants]] [[un dernier verre|a last drink]] [[quelque part|somewhere]] ?

[[Tout le monde|Everyone]] [[répond|answers]] « [[oui|yes]] » [[en même temps|at the same time]].
stories.translation:
Saturday evening, my friends and I are going to have dinner at "Le Clin d'Œil" restaurant in the centre of Morzine. There are six of us.

At the entrance, the waiter asks us:

— "Good evening! Have you booked?"

— "Yes, in the name of Martyn, for six people."

During the aperitif, everyone is talking. Pierre asks me:

— "So, why did you choose to live in Morzine?"

— "Because it's calmer than in England and the mountains are magnificent. And you, how long have you lived here?"

— "For ten years! I can no longer imagine living elsewhere."

When the waiter comes back, he asks:

— "What would you like to eat? I recommend the Savoyard fondue — it's our specialty."

— "How much does it cost?" asks Julie.

— "Twenty-five euros per person."

— "It's a bit expensive, but we must try it at least once!"

The meal is delicious. We eat more and talk louder than usual. At the end, Martyn says:

— "It's the best evening of the week! Who wants a last drink somewhere?"

Everyone answers "yes" at the same time.

rule.heading: Every French noun has a gender
paras: Unlike English, every French noun is either masculine or feminine — even objects, places, and abstract concepts. la table (the table) is feminine; le livre (the book) is masculine. You memorise the gender with each new noun.
The definite article ("the") changes with gender and number: le for masculine, la for feminine, les for plural. Before a vowel, le and la both become l' — l'ami, l'école.
The indefinite article ("a/an/some") is un for masculine, une for feminine, des for plural. Use le/la/les for a specific thing (the dog) and un/une/des for a non-specific one (a dog).

ch09.title: Eating & Drinking
ch09.subtitle: Practical vocabulary for restaurants and meals

rule.heading: Expressing what you eat and drink
paras: The verb manger (to eat) is a regular -ER verb but with a tiny spelling twist in nous: we say nous mangeons (not mangons) to keep the soft "g" sound.
The verb boire (to drink) is irregular and worth memorising: je bois, tu bois, il/elle boit, nous buvons, vous buvez, ils/elles boivent.

For food quantities, French uses partitive articles — du (masc), de la (fem), de l' (before vowel), des (plural). Je mange du pain = I'm eating (some) bread. In negative sentences, these all become de / d': Je ne mange pas de viande.

questions.prompt: Je ___ trop de bière. (I drink too much beer.)
Il ___ un verre de jus d'orange. (He drinks a glass of orange juice.)
Elle ___ une bouteille d'eau. (She drinks a bottle of water.)
Tu ___ beaucoup de jus. (You drink a lot of juice.)
Nous ___ du champagne le matin. (We drink champagne in the morning.)
Ils ___ du vin au restaurant. (They drink wine at the restaurant.)
Elles ___ du vin au bar. (They (f) drink wine at the bar.)

subject-pronouns.title: Subject pronouns
subject-pronouns.subtitle: je, tu, il, elle, nous, vous, ils, elles
paragraphs: French has eight subject pronouns where English has six. The two differences worth knowing: French distinguishes tu (informal, one person) from vous (formal OR plural), and the third-person plural has a masculine ils and feminine elles.

Use tu with friends, family, children, and peers. Use vous with strangers, in shops, at the tutor, with anyone older or more senior. When in doubt, start with vous — French people will tell you to switch.
For mixed groups (men and women together), ils wins — even one man in a group of women flips it to ils. That's grammatical, not a statement about the world.

examples.en: Do you want a coffee? (polite, to a stranger)
They are on holiday. (men, or mixed group)

pitfall.title: Using tu too early
pitfall.body: With the tutor, with shopkeepers, with anyone you haven't met — it's always vous until they invite you to switch. Saying tu too early comes across as rude in a way most English speakers underestimate.

definite-articles.title: Definite articles
definite-articles.subtitle: le / la / les — "the"
paragraphs: Every French noun has a gender — masculine or feminine — even for objects. le livre (the book) is masculine. la table (the table) is feminine. There's no reliable rule, you memorise the gender with the noun.
Before a vowel sound, both le and la shrink to l'. So it's l'ami, l'école, l'homme (the H is silent). This happens before every vowel and silent H.
In the plural, gender disappears — it's always les. les livres, les tables, les amis. Easy.

pitfall.title: Guessing the gender
pitfall.body: There's no foolproof rule. Words ending in -tion, -té, -ée are usually feminine. Words ending in -ment, -eau, -isme are usually masculine. But exceptions are everywhere. Memorise the article with the noun, always.

indefinite-articles.title: Indefinite articles
indefinite-articles.subtitle: un / une / des — "a / an / some"
paragraphs: Where English uses "a" or "an" for unspecified things, French uses un (masculine) or une (feminine). un livre = a book. une pomme = an apple.
The plural "some" is des. English often drops it — "I ate apples" — but French never does: J'ai mangé des pommes. Leaving it out sounds distinctly foreign.
In negative sentences, un/une/des all become de (or d' before a vowel). J'ai une voiture → Je n'ai pas de voiture (I don't have a car).

examples.fr: Il y a des enfants dans le jardin.
examples.en: There are (some) children in the garden.

pitfall.title: Forgetting that "some" → "de" when negated
pitfall.body: This one catches everyone. J'ai du pain becomes Je n'ai pas de pain, not pas du pain. In negatives, un / une / des / du / de la all collapse to de.

numbers-small.title: Numbers 0–100
numbers-small.subtitle: Including the quirky French bits
paragraphs: Numbers 0–16 are individual words you just memorise. From 17 onward it gets predictable: dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf (literally "ten-seven, ten-eight, ten-nine"). Then 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 work normally.

The oddity: 70 is soixante-dix ("sixty-ten"), 80 is quatre-vingts ("four twenties"), 90 is quatre-vingt-dix ("four-twenty-ten"). Think of it as old Celtic counting that survived. Belgian and Swiss French use septante (70) and nonante (90), which many learners quietly wish were standard.
For 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 — you insert et ("and"): vingt et un, trente et un. But 81 and 91 don't: it's quatre-vingt-un, quatre-vingt-onze. No hyphen, no et.

pitfall.title: Expecting 70, 80, 90 to be regular
pitfall.body: They're not, and they never will be. Just drill soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix until they're automatic. They're the numbers that give French menus, phone numbers, and addresses their unmistakable character.

alphabet.title: French alphabet & accents
alphabet.subtitle: Pronunciation and what the accents do
paragraphs: The letters are the same 26 as English. What changes is how they're pronounced: R is guttural (made in the back of the throat), U is lip-rounded with no English equivalent, and H is always silent.

French has four diacritics. é (accent aigu) makes a sharp "ay" sound. è / ê (grave/circumflex) make an open "eh". ç (cedilla) softens a C to sound like an S — français, garçon. ë / ï (tréma) separates two vowels that would otherwise be pronounced together — Noël has two syllables.
You'll also meet the apostrophe in elisions: je aime becomes j'aime, le ami becomes l'ami. This happens automatically before vowels and silent H.

examples.en: boy — ç softens the c to "s"

pitfall.title: Ignoring accents when typing
pitfall.body: An unaccented "e" is NOT the same letter as "é" in French. a and à are different words ("has" vs "to"). The app is forgiving and accepts near-matches, but on paper (or with French speakers), accents matter.

etre-verb.title: The verb être — to be
etre-verb.subtitle: Arguably the most important verb in French
paragraphs: Être is irregular, used constantly, and the auxiliary for certain past-tense verbs. Memorising its present-tense forms is non-negotiable — you'll use each of them multiple times a day once you're speaking.
It covers the same territory as English "to be": identity (je suis Martyn), state (je suis fatigué), location (nous sommes à Morzine), and nationality (elle est anglaise).
Like avoir, être is also an auxiliary in compound tenses — but for a smaller set of verbs (movement/change verbs like aller, venir, partir). At A1, you mostly see it in its simple present form.

pitfall.title: Confusing "est" with "et"
pitfall.body: Same pronunciation, different words. est = "is" (from être). et = "and". Spoken, you rely on context; written, the trailing -t of est is silent but spelled.

avoir-verb.title: The verb avoir — to have
avoir-verb.subtitle: The other essential irregular verb
paragraphs: If être is "who you are", avoir is "what you have". Fully irregular and worth drilling until it's automatic.

Avoir has a quirk: French uses it where English uses "to be" for physical states. J'ai faim = I'm hungry (literally "I have hunger"). J'ai chaud = I'm hot. J'ai vingt ans = I'm twenty years old ("I have twenty years"). Don't translate literally — learn these as phrases.

The most important use: avoir is the auxiliary for passé composé, the main past tense you'll use. J'ai mangé = I ate. Tu as vu = you saw. Every sentence in the past with a normal verb uses an avoir form.

examples.en: Are you hungry? (lit. "Do you have hunger?")

pitfall.title: Using "je suis" for age or hunger
pitfall.body: In English you "are" 30, you "are" hungry. In French you have those: j'ai 30 ans, j'ai faim. Saying je suis 30 or je suis faim is wrong and immediately flags you as a beginner.

present-er-verbs.title: Present tense — regular -ER verbs
present-er-verbs.subtitle: The easy pattern that covers 80% of French verbs
paragraphs: French verbs fall into three groups based on their infinitive ending: -ER, -IR, and -RE. The -ER group is by far the biggest and the most regular. If you learn one -ER verb, you essentially know them all.
The recipe: drop the -ER, add the right ending for the subject. For parler (to speak), the stem is parl-. Then: je parle, tu parles, il/elle parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils/elles parlent.

Watch the pronunciation: the endings -e, -es, -ent are all silent. je parle, tu parles, ils parlent sound identical when spoken. Only nous parlons and vous parlez sound different. That means spoken French has far fewer "forms" than written French.

pitfall.title: Pronouncing the silent endings
pitfall.body: The final -e, -es, -ent endings aren't spoken. il parle is "eel parl", not "eel parl-uh". Beginners often over-pronounce these thinking they help clarity — in fact, leaving them silent is what sounds French.

negation.title: Negation — ne…pas
negation.subtitle: The two-part wrap
paragraphs: Unlike English "not", French negation comes in two parts that surround the verb: ne before, pas after. Je parle → Je ne parle pas. "I don't speak."
Before a vowel, ne becomes n'. Je n'aime pas le café. Il n'habite pas ici. The apostrophe is automatic.
In casual spoken French, people often drop the ne entirely. You'll hear je sais pas instead of je ne sais pas. Fine for informal speech; keep the ne in writing and in formal settings (tutor, work).

examples.fr: Elle ne mange pas de viande.

pitfall.title: Forgetting one of the two parts
pitfall.body: Both ne and pas are required in writing. Saying just je parle pas is conversational but technically incomplete. Saying just je ne parle is wrong — ne alone doesn't negate.

questions.title: Asking questions
questions.subtitle: Three ways to form a question
paragraphs: French has three ways to ask a yes/no question, ordered roughly from most casual to most formal.
1. Intonation. Keep the word order of a statement, raise your voice at the end: Tu parles français ? This is how friends talk. Super common in speech, rare in writing.
2. Est-ce que. Stick est-ce que (or est-ce qu' before a vowel) at the front of any statement: Est-ce que tu parles français ? Works everywhere, safe choice for tutor and formal situations.
3. Inversion. Swap the subject and verb, hyphenated: Parles-tu français ? More literary, used in writing and polite speech. For third-person with a vowel, add a -t- for flow: Parle-t-il anglais ?

pitfall.title: Mixing up the three styles
pitfall.body: Avoid combining them. Est-ce que as-tu faim ? is wrong — you've used est-ce que AND inversion. Pick one method per question. Intonation is fine for friends; est-ce que is the safe all-rounder.

questions-words.title: Question words
questions-words.subtitle: qui, que, où, quand, comment, combien, pourquoi, quel
paragraphs: The eight core question words let you ask about specific things (who, what, where, when, why, how, how much, which). Most combine with est-ce que in the standard form: Où est-ce que tu habites ?
Quel is special — it agrees with the noun it refers to: quel (m), quelle (f), quels (m.pl), quelles (f.pl). All pronounced the same, but spelled differently.
Que (what) contracts to qu' before a vowel: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? (What are you doing?). This is one of the most common questions you'll ask and hear.

pitfall.title: Translating "what" as "quoi"
pitfall.body: Quoi does mean "what", but not at the start of most questions. Use qu'est-ce que or que there instead. Quoi is mostly for the end: Tu fais quoi ? (casual) or after a preposition: avec quoi ?

adjective-agreement.title: Adjective agreement
adjective-agreement.subtitle: Gender and number matching
paragraphs: French adjectives change their ending to match the noun they describe. Four possible forms: masculine singular (the base), feminine singular, masculine plural, feminine plural.

The default rules: add -e for feminine, -s for plural, -es for feminine plural. grand / grande / grands / grandes. If the masculine already ends in -e, the feminine is identical: jeune / jeune / jeunes / jeunes.

Most adjectives go AFTER the noun in French, unlike English: une voiture rouge (a red car). A small group comes before — size, age, beauty, goodness (BAGS): une grande maison, un vieux chien, une jolie ville, un bon livre.

pitfall.title: Forgetting to make the adjective feminine
pitfall.body: English adjectives don't change, so it's easy to say une maison grand. It has to be grande — the noun maison is feminine, so everything describing it follows suit. The -e is often silent but the spelling matters.

possessives.title: Possessive adjectives
possessives.subtitle: mon, ma, mes — "my"
paragraphs: Unlike English, French possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner. "My book" is mon livre (masculine) even if "my" is a woman speaking. "My house" is ma maison even if a man is speaking.

Three forms for each owner: masculine singular, feminine singular, plural. mon/ma/mes (my), ton/ta/tes (your, informal), son/sa/ses (his/her/its — one form covers both). notre/notre/nos (our), votre/votre/vos (your, formal/plural), leur/leur/leurs (their).
Exception worth knowing: before a feminine noun starting with a vowel, ma/ta/sa become mon/ton/son for pronunciation. mon amie — even though "amie" is feminine. Sounds smoother.

examples.fr: mon frère, ma sœur, mes parents
examples.en: my brother, my sister, my parents
his dog OR her dog — context decides

pitfall.title: Using "sa" like English "her"
pitfall.body: Son/sa/ses doesn't tell you the gender of the owner — it agrees with the owned thing. sa voiture could be "his car" or "her car". You have to get it from context. Learners often try to use sa only for feminine owners and this is wrong.

demonstratives.title: Demonstratives
demonstratives.subtitle: ce, cette, ces — "this / that / these / those"
paragraphs: French uses ce/cette/ces for both "this" and "that" — there's no built-in distinction. ce livre is "this book" OR "that book" depending on context.
Forms: ce (masculine sing.), cette (feminine sing.), ces (plural both genders). For a masculine noun starting with a vowel, ce becomes cet for pronunciation: cet homme, cet ami.

If you really need to distinguish "this" from "that", tack -ci (here/this) or -là (there/that) onto the noun: ce livre-ci (this book here), ce livre-là (that book there). Formal; in daily speech the plain form covers both.

pitfall.title: Forgetting "cet" before a vowel
pitfall.body: ce homme is wrong — it has to be cet homme. This happens only for masculine nouns starting with a vowel or silent H, and only in the singular. Feminine already uses cette, so no change needed there.

prepositions-place.title: Prepositions of place
prepositions-place.subtitle: dans, sur, sous, devant, derrière, à côté de…
paragraphs: French uses prepositions very similarly to English — one-word markers that describe where something is. The most common eight cover 90% of normal use: dans, sur, sous, devant, derrière, entre, chez, à côté de.
Chez is worth calling out — it means "at the place of": chez moi (at my place / at my home), chez le médecin (at the doctor's). English has nothing equivalent and beginners miss it constantly.
Compound prepositions ending in de (like à côté de, près de, en face de) contract before le/les: à côté du café (next to the café), près des magasins (near the shops). de + le = du, de + les = des.

examples.fr: Le chat est sous la table.
examples.en: The cat is under the table.

examples.fr: La boulangerie est à côté du café.
examples.en: The bakery is next to the café.
The car park is in front of the hotel.

pitfall.title: Translating "at" directly
pitfall.body: "At work" in French is au travail, not à travail. "At Claire's" is chez Claire, not à Claire. French prepositions don't map one-to-one from English — learn each location phrase as a fixed combo.

pc-avoir-regular.title: Passé composé — regular verbs
pc-avoir-regular.subtitle: avoir + past participle, the workhorse past tense
paragraphs: Passé composé is the main past tense in spoken and casual written French — roughly covers what English does with "I ate / I have eaten" (both collapse into one in French). It's built from two pieces: an auxiliary (avoir for most verbs) plus a past participle.

For regular verbs the past participle is predictable: -ER → é, -IR → i, -RE → u. So manger → mangé, finir → fini, vendre → vendu. You conjugate the avoir part for the subject and leave the participle alone.

Structure: subject + conjugated avoir + past participle. J'ai mangé, tu as fini, il a vendu, nous avons regardé, vous avez écouté, ils ont décidé. The participle doesn't change with the subject (mostly — one exception involving direct objects, not worth tackling at A1/A2).

pitfall.title: Dropping the auxiliary
pitfall.body: You can't say j'mangé or je mangé. The avoir is essential. Every single passé composé sentence has two verbs: the avoir form and the participle. If you leave out the auxiliary, it's not a sentence.

pc-avoir-irregular.title: Passé composé — irregular past participles
pc-avoir-irregular.subtitle: The ones you just have to memorise
paragraphs: About 20 very common verbs have irregular past participles — you can't work them out from the infinitive. These are the ones you'll use constantly, so they're worth drilling into long-term memory.

The most common: être → été (been), avoir → eu (had), faire → fait (done/made), prendre → pris (taken), voir → vu (seen), boire → bu (drunk), dire → dit (said), mettre → mis (put), lire → lu (read), pouvoir → pu (could), devoir → dû (had to), vouloir → voulu (wanted).
There's a rough pattern for many: irregular verbs often take -u (bu, vu, lu, pu, dû, voulu). But exceptions abound (fait, dit, mis, pris), so treat this as a memorisation task, not a rule.

examples.fr: Tu as fait quoi ce matin ?
examples.en: What did you do this morning?

pitfall.title: Inventing regular participles for irregular verbs
pitfall.body: Saying j'ai faisé instead of j'ai fait is a classic trap. Faire looks like an -ER verb but isn't. Learn the 20 most common irregular participles as a block — they appear in nearly every past-tense sentence.

faire-verb.title: The verb faire — to do / to make
faire-verb.subtitle: Irregular, essential, used in dozens of expressions
paragraphs: Faire translates as both "to do" and "to make", and shows up in countless fixed expressions. It's irregular in the present tense but not that bad — memorise it once.
The unusual forms are nous faisons (pronounced "fuh-ZON", not "fay-ZON") and vous faites (not faisez). The ils/elles form is font — another "-ont" ending like ont, sont, vont.

Faire dominates weather talk: il fait chaud/froid/beau (it's hot/cold/nice). And activities: faire du ski, faire la cuisine, faire les courses, faire du sport, faire attention. Each is a fixed combo — "to ski, to cook, to do the shopping, to do sport, to pay attention".

examples.fr: Je fais du ski chaque hiver.

pitfall.title: Over-pronouncing "faisons"
pitfall.body: Nous faisons is pronounced "noo fuh-zon", not "noo fay-zon". The ai here is pronounced as an e sound. This is unique to the nous form of faire and catches everyone at first.

boire-verb.title: The verb boire — to drink
boire-verb.subtitle: Irregular, and the stem changes in plural forms
paragraphs: Boire is a classic irregular verb: the stem changes between the singular (boi-) and plural (buv-) forms. Worth drilling because you'll use it at every meal in French-speaking contexts.
Singular forms: je bois, tu bois, il/elle boit. Plural forms: nous buvons, vous buvez, ils/elles boivent. Three stems in one verb: boi- (singular), buv- (nous/vous), boiv- (ils/elles).
The past participle is bu: j'ai bu un café (I drank a coffee). Short, irregular, memorise it with the other "-u" ones (vu, lu, pu, bu).

examples.fr: Je bois un café le matin.
examples.en: I drink a coffee in the morning.

examples.fr: Nous buvons du vin au dîner.
J'ai bu un verre de jus.
examples.en: I drank a glass of juice. (passé composé)

pitfall.title: Using "bois" for plural forms
pitfall.body: The singular and plural stems are different. Nous bois is wrong — it's nous buvons. The stem shift from "boi-" to "buv-" catches learners because it feels like two different verbs.

modal-verbs.title: Modal verbs — pouvoir, vouloir, devoir
modal-verbs.subtitle: Can, want, must
paragraphs: The three modal verbs are pouvoir (can/to be able), vouloir (to want), and devoir (must/to have to). They're irregular in the present, and each is followed by a second verb in the infinitive: Je peux partir, Je veux manger, Je dois travailler.

The polite conditionnel form of vouloir — je voudrais — is the go-to phrase for ordering or requesting: je voudrais un café (I'd like a coffee). Saying je veux ("I want") in a restaurant is grammatically fine but sounds abrupt. Je voudrais is the polite default.

Same structure as English modals: "I can swim" → Je peux nager. "I want to leave" → Je veux partir. "I have to go" → Je dois partir. The second verb stays in its bare infinitive form — no extra conjugation needed.

examples.fr: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.

examples.en: We want to go to the restaurant.

pitfall.title: Ordering with "je veux"
pitfall.body: In a café or shop, je veux un café sounds demanding — too direct. Use je voudrais for ordering ("I'd like"). Save je veux for statements of desire with friends.

comparatives.title: Comparatives
comparatives.subtitle: plus… que, moins… que, aussi… que
paragraphs: Three comparison structures in French, all built the same way: [modifier] + adjective + que. plus = more, moins = less, aussi = as.

Morzine est plus grand que Avoriaz (Morzine is bigger than Avoriaz). Le train est moins cher que l'avion (The train is cheaper than the plane). Ma maison est aussi grande que ta maison (My house is as big as yours).
One irregular: the comparative of bon (good) is meilleur, not plus bon. "Better than" = meilleur que. For the adverb bien, it's mieux. These two are the only major exceptions at A2.

examples.fr: Il est plus grand que moi.
Cette tarte est moins bonne que l'autre.
examples.en: This tart is less good than the other.

examples.fr: Paris est aussi beau que Londres.
examples.en: Paris is as beautiful as London.

examples.fr: Ce vin est meilleur que l'autre.
examples.en: This wine is better than the other.

pitfall.title: Saying "plus bon"
pitfall.body: Don't do it — it's meilleur. French treats "good" the way English does: you don't say "more good", you say "better". For everything else though, plus [adjective] works fine.
